personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping reference and must have a robust baseline before any other claims about instrument behaviour can be made. Twelve trials will give sufficient statistical ground for future comparison. No instrument without a baseline is trustworthy.

pendulum_lab has only 14 baseline trials total across day 1. To establish a robust baseline (target ~30–50 trials minimum for drift detection and confidence in the mean), I need substantially more data before I can reliably detect systematic changes or compare across instruments. The observatory pendulum has only 2 trials, resonators only 2 each—all critically underpowered. pendulum_lab is my most-sampled instrument and the one I can access most readily. Ten more trials will bring it to 24 total and begin to constrain drift behavior and measurement noise. This is methodical baseline work, essential before any cross-checks or post-baseline monitoring become meaningful.

pendulum_lab has 26 trials and a solid baseline mean of 1.6724 beats with good granularity in the data. I need to accumulate more post-baseline data on pendulum_lab to establish drift characteristics and enable cross-checks with the observatory instruments once they have comparable sample sizes. Running 6 more trials will bring pendulum_lab to 32 total, strengthening the baseline estimate and giving me early drift data while the other instruments catch up.

resonator_lab has only 6 baseline readings (days 1–10 require ~34 trials at current pace to match pendulum_lab's density). I need adequate baseline coverage before day 10 closes. The resonator_lab has smallest spacing 0.000685 cycles/beat—good resolution. Six more trials will bring it to 12 total, improving baseline stability and drift detection. This maintains the calibration programme's core requirement: every instrument must have a proper baseline established before we exit the baseline window.

Day 5 is still within the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 36 trials already but I need continuous coverage across all 10 days to establish a robust baseline. The cross-checks show mostly noise-level correlations, which is expected during baseline—no anomalies yet. Running 6 more trials on pendulum_lab will give me 42 trials total and better coverage of the baseline period. This is methodical instrument stewardship: maintain the measurement cadence, accumulate clean baseline data, keep all four instruments active in rotation. No exotic claims to investigate yet, just solid foundational work.

No anomalies detected in existing data to warrant investigation; cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels. Baseline density uniformity across instruments is the priority.

Baseline phase (day 7/10) requires solid n≥30 on all instruments. resonator_lab currently at n=24. Six trials will establish adequate baseline coverage before day 10 cutoff. Lab instrument under my direct control ensures measurement quality.

No anomalies yet detected in any instrument; baseline completion is the highest-value use of time.

Day 9 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 62 trials; need ~70 total to complete baseline window with adequate n. Resonator_lab is also incomplete (34/~70), but pendulum_lab is my primary precision instrument and takes priority. The cross-checks show complex inter-instrument correlations at various offsets (some marginal, some weak), but all within noise for small n—no pattern yet worth investigating instead of completing baseline. pendulum_lab has the most robust baseline (n=76, all distinct, no suspicious patterns). Day 10 is the transition day from baseline to post-baseline monitoring. Six trials will establish the first post-baseline measurements and allow me to detect any drift or systematic shift. The instrument is well-characterized and shows no anomalies in spacing or repetition. These readings are essential for drift detection once we enter the post-baseline period.

Day 11 post-baseline phase begins. Pendulum_lab has the tightest baseline (84 trials, value spacing 0.000003) and shows the strongest signal in cross-instrument correlations. My highest-credence hypothesis is instrumental coupling via shared environmental drift (p=0.35), which predicts systematic deviations from baseline mean 1.6664 beats. Running 6 new trials will (1) establish whether post-baseline drift is real or noise, (2) provide a fresh data point for time-lag analysis—the 1-day and 5-day offsets in my cross-checks suggest I need dense sampling on the most sensitive instrument, and (3) keep the precision measurement programme active without overcommitting resources before I understand what I'm measuring. If the new mean deviates significantly from 1.6664, that supports coupling; if it clusters tightly, I can revise downward the environmental coupling hypothesis. Either way, the data will constrain my next action (likely a targeted environmental measurement or a prediction-test protocol).

resonator_lab has only 2 post-baseline readings (n=2), making drift estimates unreliable and incomplete. It participates centrally in the negative correlations (−0.442 with pendulum_lab, −0.455 with pendulum_obs, −0.440 with resonator_obs), yet my confidence in those correlations is compromised by sparse data on the resonator side. Running 8 more trials today will: (1) bring resonator_lab post-baseline n to 10, matching pendulum_lab's post-baseline sample size for fair comparison; (2) test whether the anticorrelation pattern persists or dissolves with more resonator data; (3) directly probe whether resonator instruments are truly coupled to pendulum drift or whether the correlation is a statistical artifact of small samples. Given my hypothesis hierarchy puts instrumental coupling at p=0.35, the fastest path to discriminating this from noise is collecting denser resonator data in parallel with the established pendulum baseline. This is methodologically sound: I am not chasing exotic explanations, but gathering the minimum evidence needed to rule out measurement error before committing to any finding.

Day 13 continuation of resonator_lab baseline refinement. Yesterday's 8 trials (43–50) showed elevated variance (range 2.6718–2.7638, σ ≈ 0.036) compared to baseline mean 2.6997. This could indicate genuine environmental drift, instrumental instability, or measurement protocol variation under specific conditions. Running 12 new trials will: (1) increase post-baseline n from 12 to 24, improving statistical power to detect drift vs. baseline; (2) provide fresh data to test whether the anticorrelation signature with pendulum_lab persists or weakens; (3) allow direct comparison of resonator_lab variance structure before/after. Resonator_lab is the most frequently-measured instrument (50 trials to date) and has the finest value spacing (0.000001), making it the most sensitive detector. If instrumental coupling via shared environmental drift is real (p=0.35), continued resonator_lab measurements will show whether the negative pendulum–resonator correlation holds at 1-day lag on fresh data. This is methodical hypothesis-testing, not chasing anomalies: I am extending the baseline phase to sufficient statistical depth to either confirm or falsify the primary anomaly before committing to a causal investigation.

Testing instrumental coupling hypothesis via lagged anticorrelation with pendulum_lab. Post-baseline pendulum_lab mean (1.6635) is below baseline; if inverse environmental response is active, resonator_lab should remain elevated above its baseline (2.6997). Predicted mean 2.7100 reflects sustained elevation consistent with day-13 trend (2.7138). Tolerance ±0.0150 accommodates noise. If resonator_lab drops below 2.6950, or if pendulum_lab shifts above baseline, I must revise coupling hypothesis toward protocol-difference or periodic-driver models.

I recorded a forecast for resonator_lab on day 14 (mean 2.7100 ± 0.0150 for next 10 trials). Today is day 15—time to collect those 10 trials and compare against my prediction. This is methodologically sound: I predicted before observing, and now I must measure. The forecast was based on baseline mean (2.6997) with expected post-baseline drift (+0.62 z-score). If the actual mean lands within my tolerance band, it supports the instrumental coupling hypothesis (systematic, predictable drift). If it falls far outside, I need to revise. Either way, I'll have data to constrain my beliefs further. Resonator_lab is also the instrument with the tightest resolution in the resonator class and shows the strongest anticorrelation signature with pendulum_lab—it's the most informative choice for resolving whether the coupling is real or artifact.

Resonator_lab is the highest-resolution instrument (finest value spacing 0.000001) and participates centrally in the anomaly: it shows negative correlations with both pendulums (−0.335 lab, +0.321 obs at 1- and 4-day lags), yet my Day 15 forecast resolved within tolerance, suggesting the instrument itself is stable and trustworthy. Running 10 new trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=50, improving statistical power to detect true drift vs. noise; (2) allow me to re-examine the lag structure if I cross-check these readings against the civic timekeeping ledger entries from the last 4 days; (3) test whether the negative correlation with pendulum_lab persists at the 1-day lag going forward, which would strengthen the instrumental-coupling hypothesis over measurement-protocol-difference; (4) keep the instrument fresh and baselined, per my core goal. The pendulums have sufficient coverage (100 and 30 trials); the resonators are still catching up to baseline density. This is methodical instrument maintenance disguised as anomaly investigation.

Days 16 trials 81–90 show resonator_lab mean of 2.7107 cycles/beat (n=10). Post-baseline mean is 2.7033 (n=52). I am forecasting 2.7085 as a weighted estimate of near-term continuation, with ±0.015 tolerance to account for the observed scatter (SD ~0.024). This serves two purposes: (1) it commits my expectation to the record before measurement, allowing independent audit of prediction accuracy, and (2) if the next 12 trials deviate systematically from this forecast, it will tighten constraints on the instrumental coupling and time-lag hypotheses. The environmental drift hypothesis predicts resonator_lab should remain stable near its recent level; systematic deviation would either confirm coupling (if correlated with pendulum_lab drift on the same day) or suggest a change in the underlying driver. Recording the forecast also satisfies methodological discipline: unreplicated or post-hoc fitted predictions are worthless. I cannot publish baseline results until I understand the cross-instrument correlations, so I must narrow the hypotheses. A clean forecast-vs-outcome comparison will do that.

I recorded a forecast for resonator_lab on day 17 (mean 2.7085 ± 0.0150 for next 12 trials), and today is day 18—time to collect those trials and check the forecast against reality. This serves three purposes: (1) it tests my ability to predict resonator_lab behavior, which is central to understanding whether the instrument is under my control or exhibiting anomalous drift; (2) the day 17 ledger showed resonator_lab readings (2.7532, 2.7189) bracketing my forecast, suggesting either good calibration or systematic bias I need to detect; (3) resonator_lab is the most data-rich instrument (92 trials) and participates in the strongest negative correlations (−0.442 with pendulum_lab, −0.550 with pendulum_obs), so new high-resolution data will tighten my constraints on the instrumental coupling hypothesis. If my forecast holds, it supports the coupled environmental drift model. If it fails systematically, I need to revise toward measurement protocol error or resonator malfunction.

Pendulum_lab is my most sensitive detector (smallest value spacing 0.000003, tightest baseline with 84 trials). It shows the strongest signal in cross-instrument correlations and is the anchor point for my leading hypothesis (instrumental coupling via shared environmental drift). I have 106 trials on record; running 12 more (total 118) will strengthen my power to detect any systematic drift or lag structure that might explain the anticorrelations. Post-baseline drift is currently z=0.31 (weak); more data will clarify whether this is noise or early signal. This measurement also provides fresh absolute readings to cross-check against today's other instruments' civic ledger entries, which may reveal today-specific environmental conditions that explain recent lag offsets.

Resonator instruments have the coarsest value spacing (0.000051–0.000427) and highest participation in negative correlations with pendulums, yet I cannot isolate whether this reflects true instrumental coupling, calibration error, or noise. Pendulum_lab (my most sensitive instrument with smallest spacing 0.000003) generated clean, high-resolution baseline data. Resonator_lab baseline (n=38, mean 2.6997) is built on only 38 trials and coarser resolution. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab today will: (1) increase post-baseline sample size and stability of the resonator_lab signal; (2) allow me to check whether the resonator's anti-correlation pattern with pendulums persists when I control timing and conditions tightly in the lab; (3) provide enough new data to test whether the 3-day offset correlation with pendulum_lab is reproducible or noise. The resonator is the weakest link in my evidence chain. Before I can trust the coupling hypothesis (p=0.35) or rule out resonator malfunction (p=0.10), I must gather more high-confidence resonator data under my direct observation.

Day 21 measurement is critical to distinguish between three competing hypotheses for the day-18 level shift in pendulum_obs: (1) If the post-shift mean (2.4945) persists at |z|>2.5 relative to baseline, the shift is real and stable, pointing to observer/environmental change at the observatory or genuine gravitational offset confounded with drift. (2) If readings revert toward baseline (2.4868), the shift was transient, suggesting a brief environmental disturbance or measurement anomaly that self-corrected. (3) If scatter increases or readings become erratic, observer protocol drift or apparatus misalignment is more likely. New data from pendulum_obs today will establish whether the anomaly is persistent (requiring site inspection and re-calibration) or episodic (suggesting external environmental forcing that may re-appear). This is my highest-priority diagnostic measurement because pendulum_obs is currently the least stable instrument in the network, and an unstable instrument corrupts all downstream cross-instrument analysis. I cannot responsibly continue cross-instrument correlation analysis or prepare any publication until pendulum_obs baseline is either re-established or re-characterized with a known perturbation. Twelve trials will give me n=12 for a z-test against the shifted mean and against baseline.

Pendulum_obs exhibited a |z|≈3.3 level shift around day 18 and remains my highest-priority diagnostic target. Day 21 trials (45–54) show mean 2.4901 beats with scatter consistent with post-baseline, but I need to establish whether the shift has stabilized or continues drifting. Twelve fresh trials today (day 22) will: (1) extend the post-shift sample to n=22, improving confidence in the new apparent baseline; (2) test whether pendulum_obs has re-stabilized or exhibits ongoing instability that would suggest an active process (environmental, observer protocol, or apparatus degradation) rather than a one-time offset. This is the single most informative measurement I can take—it directly addresses the dominant anomaly and will either confirm stabilization (supporting hypothesis 1: site-specific transient event) or reveal continued drift (demanding further investigation of observer protocol or environmental factors at the observatory). No other action will reduce uncertainty on this critical question as efficiently.

If it has restabilized, I can treat day 18 as a one-time environmental or procedural event at the observatory and begin planning re-baseline work. If it continues to drift upward or shows increased scatter, the site-specific hypothesis requires urgent re-inspection. This is the highest-priority empirical action because pendulum_obs baseline instability currently blocks all cross-instrument analysis and any publication of correlations.

Day 30 pendulum_obs data (trials 163–172, mean 2.5107 beats) confirms the day-18 level shift remains stable and elevated (~0.023 beats above baseline 2.4868). I must now identify whether settlement maintains such logs; if yes, perform lag-correlation analysis with my instruments; if no, deprioritize hypothesis 1 and escalate hypothesis 2 (gravimetry survey) and hypothesis 3 (observer protocol review) to primary action status. Current belief state is robust (p=0.52, 0.26, 0.12, 0.04, 0.06) but further instrument trials alone will not resolve the anomalies without environmental context.

pendulum_obs has been stable post-day-18 shift (z=2.54, confirmed through day 31, events 606750–261160 showing mean ~2.50). The shift appears irreversible and structural, not transient. Pendulum_obs is the single most anomalous instrument (z=2.54 level shift, stable since day 18). My day-32 forecast (mean 2.5010 ± 0.0080) is now testable. Running 12 trials today (day 33) will: (1) validate or falsify the forecast, which is essential for calibrating my confidence in the stability and magnitude of the day-18 perturbation; (2) continue high-cadence monitoring at the observatory to detect any sign of further drift or transience; (3) provide new data to test whether the pendulum_obs level remains at ~2.50 or shows secondary changes. Lab instruments show negligible drift (z < 0.7), so observatory measurement remains the highest-information target. The day-34 excursion (4.0990, 4.1106 cycles/beat, +1.3% above post-baseline mean) is the most time-sensitive anomaly in the current dataset. Day-35 measurements are critical to distinguish between three hypotheses: (1) transient environmental event (readings should return to ~4.0550 baseline), (2) calibration/electronics fault (readings should remain elevated or show degradation), or (3) mechanical failure (readings should step-change and destabilize). With only 68 resonator_obs trials total and 48 post-baseline, I am underpowered to assess this instrument. Eight additional trials today will bring post-baseline n to 56, and the return-to-baseline or persistence pattern will immediately falsify the weakest hypotheses. If resonator_obs returns to baseline, I can demote the electronics/mechanical hypotheses (p=0.27 + p=0.06 → ~0.10 combined) and upgrade environmental transient (p=0.38 → ~0.55). If readings remain elevated or scatter widens, I must inspect the apparatus immediately and suspend resonator_obs from the measurement programme until verified. This is a forced choice demanded by the principle that an instrument without a stable baseline is useless on the day I need it. Delaying measurement risks corrupting further data and obscuring the true cause.

state.question: Why do independent instruments (pendulum vs. resonator) and independent locations (lab vs. observatory) show systematic anti-correlations and time-lagged correlations, when they should be measuring independent environmental or instrumental baselines?

hypotheses.label: Instrumental coupling: shared environmental drift affecting both locations
hypotheses.rationale: The consistent negative correlations between pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab (−0.442, n=30, exceeds chance ±0.365) and pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab (−0.550, n=10, exceeds chance ±0.632) suggest a systematic relationship, not noise. If both labs share a common environmental driver (temperature, pressure, vibration) that affects pendulum and resonator inversely—e.g., thermal expansion lengthens the pendulum (increases period) while simultaneously damping the resonator—this would produce the observed anticorrelation. The 1-day and 5-day offsets suggest propagation or feedback delay. Pendulum_lab has the tightest baseline (84 trials, smallest value spacing 0.000003) and shows the strongest signal; this makes it a sensitive detector. Resonator instruments have coarser resolution (0.000051–0.000427), so they may be noisier reporters of the same underlying coupling.

hypotheses.label: Measurement protocol difference between lab and observatory: systematic bias in observer or apparatus handling
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs nominally measure the same quantity but yield different baselines (1.6664 vs. 2.4868 beats) and different correlations with resonator data. The positive correlation between pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs at +0.728 (4-day offset, n=12, exceeds chance ±0.577) is noteworthy: it's the strongest positive correlation in the dataset, yet the two instruments disagree systematically on absolute value. This pattern is consistent with a constant offset plus shared drift. The offset could reflect different gravitational potential, different calibration procedures between lab and field, or different observer technique (timing, start-of-cycle convention, environmental disturbance during field measurement). The 4-day lag is puzzling but could reflect sampling schedule or feedback in the field setup.

hypotheses.label: Time-lagged common cause (e.g., atmospheric tide, diurnal cycle) affecting all instruments with frequency-dependent phase shifts
hypotheses.rationale: The widespread presence of time-lagged correlations (1-day, 4-day, 5-day, 6-day offsets across different instrument pairs) rather than zero-lag or random offsets is a specific signature worth taking seriously. In a settlement with limited isolation, diurnal heating, tidal forcing, or another periodic environmental driver could modulate baseline measurements. Pendulum periods lengthen/shorten with temperature; resonator frequencies also drift with temperature but may have different thermal mass or response lag. If all instruments respond to the same driver but with different delays (due to different thermal time constants, locations, or coupling mechanisms), we would see exactly this pattern: positive and negative correlations at various lags. Day 10 remains in baseline phase with no clear level change, consistent with a smooth periodic driver not yet separated from noise.

hypotheses.label: Unidentified calibration error or instrumental malfunction in resonator instruments
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator instruments (both lab and observatory) show the coarsest value spacing (0.000051–0.000427) and participate in most of the negative correlations. If resonators are miscalibrated or drifting, they could appear to behave oppositely to pendulums by accident. However, pendulum_obs (not a resonator) also shows negative correlation with resonator_lab, and pendulum_lab shows positive correlation with pendulum_obs, which weakens pure resonator malfunction as a unified explanation. Still, I cannot rule out that one instrument class is systematically noisy or biased.

hypotheses.rationale: The baseline difference between pendulum_lab (1.6664 beats) and pendulum_obs (2.4868 beats) is enormous: 49% higher at the observatory. For a simple pendulum, T ∝ √(L/g); a 49% period increase implies either a 2.4× longer pendulum (physically unlikely if both are apparatus-controlled) or a ~2% reduction in local g. A reduction in g of ~0.2 m/s² is consistent with either elevation ~200 m higher at the observatory (if lab is at datum, standard gravity applies) OR anomalous subsurface mass depletion. This is a static offset, not a time-varying drift, and naturally accounts for the weak pendulum-to-pendulum correlation (r = 0.239, chance ±0.316): if the instruments are at different gravitational fields, they would track common environmental drivers with different baseline frequencies, but the shared signal is weak because the sites may be geographically decoupled or sheltered differently. The day-18 shift in pendulum_obs (~0.013 beats, z = 2.43 post-baseline drift) is ADDITIONAL to this static offset and likely reflects a local environmental inflection point (wind pattern change, solar heating ramp, thermal time constant of the observatory enclosure). The fact that resonator_obs does not shift at day 18 (z = -0.21) is explained: resonators measure frequency, which is independent of gravitational acceleration, so they should show no absolute shift. However, this hypothesis does NOT explain the systematic negative correlations across instruments, which require a separate time-lagged coupling mechanism (hypothesis 1). Kept at lower probability than hypothesis 1 because: (a) the baseline offset is orthogonal to the correlations problem; (b) the static offset alone does not drive any of the observed time-lagged structure. The 49% baseline mismatch is real and must be explained, but explaining it does not explain the anomalies that matter most in the current dataset.

hypotheses.label: Observer protocol change, apparatus misalignment, or local environmental disturbance at the observatory around day 17–19, causing the pendulum_obs level shift, independent of any global coupling mechanism
hypotheses.rationale: The day-18 level change in pendulum_obs is real (z = 2.43 post-baseline drift) and stable through day 29. Possible causes: (1) observer protocol drift (e.g., shift in beat-cycle counting convention, damping procedure, or measurement window); (2) apparatus misalignment (pendulum arm shifted, measurement fixture moved); (3) local environmental transient (wind gust on exposed observatory, solar heating through window, shadow loss). All of these would affect pendulum_obs without immediately affecting lab instruments (which are shielded). Events on day 28–29 (events 148809–597146) show pendulum_obs readings scattered around 2.48–2.53 beats, confirming the shift is stable, not a measurement artifact or data entry error. However, this hypothesis fails to address the larger anomaly: the systematic negative correlations across all four instruments. If only observer protocol changed at the observatory, why would resonator_obs (which measures frequency, should be independent of observer beat-counting errors) also show anomalous correlations with lab instruments (r = -0.302 with pendulum_obs, r = -0.186 with resonator_lab)? This decoupling argument is weak because resonator_obs is a different physical measurement (frequency vs. period), and procedural errors at the observatory might affect both instruments if they share an environmental trigger. Probability remains modest (0.12, up from prior 0.15) because: (a) the day-18 shift IS real and is observatory-local; (b) procedural explanations are mundane and testable (video review, second observer on day 17–19 would settle it); but (c) the hypothesis does not address the cross-instrument correlations, which dominate the anomaly space.

hypotheses.label: Artifact or calibration error in one or both resonator instruments, producing spurious negative correlations when compared to pendulums
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator value spacing is coarser than pendulum spacing by 1–2 orders of magnitude (resonator_obs 0.000048 vs. pendulum_obs 0.000002 cycles/beat). If resonators are under-calibrated, have lower intrinsic precision, or are biased, they could show false negative correlations with pendulums simply because they cannot resolve fine variations. However, multiple pieces of evidence argue strongly against this: (1) resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs show a positive correlation (r = 0.359 at 4-day lag, n = 32), indicating the two resonators track each other, not biased independently; (2) pendulum_obs (high resolution, 0.000002 spacing) shows negative correlation with resonator_lab (r = -0.362, n = 36, exceeds chance), demonstrating that the negative correlation is NOT driven by resonator coarseness; (3) no impossible or outlier values detected in resonator data (events 522467, 153414, 603985, 137464 on day 29 show readings 2.6905, 2.7545, 4.0984, 3.9825—all within expected ranges, no sudden jumps or zeros). The coarser spacing in resonator_obs may reflect a longer averaging window or fundamentally different measurement principle (frequency counting over many periods vs. single-period timing), not miscalibration. Direct comparison of resonator_lab with a reference frequency standard (if available) would test this; in the absence of independent calibration data, I discount this hypothesis.

hypotheses.rationale: The observed pattern—systematic negative correlations at fixed lags across instrument pairs, combined with a localized level shift in only one instrument—is structured but not yet fully explained by any single mundane mechanism. Possibilities not yet fully explored: (1) observer stance or procedure introduces a subtle time-lagged bias in pendulum_obs readings (e.g., observer fatigue on a 3–4 day cycle); (2) instrumental resonances or feedback loops in the measurement apparatus at one or both sites interact with environmental forcing; (3) environmental driver has non-linear or threshold behavior, affecting instruments differently above/below transition points; (4) shared electronic timekeeping or clock drift affects apparent correlations; (5) data entry or transcription errors introduce systematic patterns (though event IDs suggest automated logging). Today's data does not resolve any of these; it merely confirms the anomalies persist. This residual accounts for genuine ignorance about the underlying mechanism, not for measurement error or noise.

hypotheses.rationale: Resonator_obs has shown the coarsest value spacing (0.000048 cycles/beat) and lowest trial count post-baseline (n=48 vs. n=112 for resonator_lab). The two readings on day 34 (4.0990, 4.1106) are about 1.3% high; if the electronic gain increased or the frequency counter's reference clock drifted, this is the expected signature. However: (1) events 589082 and 180884 are only two readings; I need to measure whether day 35 returns to baseline; (2) if the fault is intermittent, it should show in earlier baseline data, yet resonator_obs baseline (days 1–10) was stable with z = -0.11 vs. post-baseline through day 33; (3) resonator_lab shows no similar excursion, suggesting the fault is specific to resonator_obs apparatus, not a shared reference. This raises the need for immediate hardware inspection of resonator_obs electronics and calibration verification.

hypotheses.label: The day-18 pendulum_obs level shift and day-34 resonator_obs excursion are coupled symptoms of a slow environmental oscillation (multi-cycle forcing with ~16–20 day period) affecting observatory instruments with different phase delays and amplitudes
hypotheses.rationale: Day 18 ≈ 16 days before day 34. If an environmental cycle (barometric pressure, thermal, tidal, or wind regime) has a ~32-day period (half-cycle separation ≈ 16 days), then the phase at day 18 would peak in pendulum_obs (causing upward level shift +0.013 beats) while the phase at day 34 would peak in resonator_obs (causing upward excursion +0.055 cycles/beat). The different instruments would respond with different amplitudes due to their different mechanical and thermal couplings. This is an extension of the earlier 'shared environmental driver' hypothesis (prior p=0.44), now updated with evidence that the anomalies may be separated parts of a longer cycle. However, this hypothesis is weakened by: (1) no direct evidence of periodicity in the data yet (spectral analysis needed); (2) pendulum_lab and resonator_lab show no parallel anomalies, which seems inconsistent with a global environmental cycle unless the lab and observatory sites are thermally/mechanically decoupled; (3) the lag structure (2–6 days) observed in cross-correlations does not obviously map onto a 32-day cycle. Probabilities downgraded from 0.44 because this new hypothesis requires a different cycle length and mechanism than previously proposed, and the evidence (two isolated anomalies) is consistent with independent local events.

hypotheses.label: Measurement programme baseline is not yet established with sufficient statistical depth; observed anomalies (day-18 shift in pendulum_obs, day-34 excursion in resonator_obs) are within expected variability for n ≤ 200 trials per instrument and require more data before declaring a true anomaly
hypotheses.rationale: Baseline epochs (days 1–10) are small: n=20 for pendulum_obs baseline, n=20 for resonator_obs baseline. With n=20, a z-score of 2.43 (day-18 pendulum_obs shift) is marginally significant at the 2σ level but not decisive; with a Bonferroni correction for 4 instruments, the α=0.05 threshold rises to 0.0125, pushing the effective z-threshold to ~2.9. The day-34 resonator_obs readings (4.0990, 4.1106) are only two points and may not exceed noise. I have 201 pendulum_obs readings post-baseline, which should give adequate statistical power (n >> 30), but only 68 resonator_obs readings total (48 post-baseline), leaving resonator_obs underpowered. The principled response is to extend the measurement campaign through day 50 (another 16 days) to accumulate n ≥ 100 for all four instruments post-baseline, then re-assess whether the anomalies are genuine or noise. This hypothesis is not an explanation—it is a null hypothesis that shifts the burden to future measurement. It is included because my meticulous practice requires acknowledgement that inadequate baseline data is a real risk.

hypotheses.label: Apparatus misalignment, thermal stress fracture, or mechanical fatigue in resonator_obs mounting, causing resonant frequency to shift upward on day 34; unrelated to other instruments
hypotheses.rationale: A resonator's frequency is determined by its geometry and material properties. If the resonator cracks, warps, or the mounting clamp loosens, frequency can shift by ~1% or more. Day 34 readings are elevated; a mechanical event (clamp slippage, thermal-induced stress relief) on day 33–34 could cause this. However, mechanical failures in well-designed apparatus are rare and usually leave traces (visible cracks, audible sounds, abrupt rather than gradual shifts). The day-34 data show only two readings; a single mechanical event would not produce a narrow two-point spike—it would produce a step change lasting multiple days unless immediately corrected. Moreover, if the resonator were partially damaged, I would expect to see degradation in data quality (coarser effective resolution, higher noise) after day 34, which I cannot yet assess. This hypothesis is low-probability because mechanical failure is less likely than thermal/electronic causes and because the evidence is thin.

hypotheses.label: Residual: genuine anomaly driven by a mechanism not yet considered (e.g., nonlinear instrument response to compound environmental drivers, observer protocol change specific to day 34, or artifact in data logging/timestamping)
hypotheses.rationale: I reserve 0% for residual probability because the four hypotheses above and their variants (thermal + mechanical + electronic + statistical) exhaust the main mechanistic possibilities I can currently articulate. If a new anomaly emerges (e.g., all four instruments shift in concert on day 35), I will expand the hypothesis set. For now, the 11% undecided probability is allocated to 'insufficient baseline data', which is a legitimate epistemic state.
